transcript.text: This is the Paper Library daily on Rare variant analysis, for Saturday, November 28.
Let's turn to rare variant analysis, where we have two new papers.

The first is a medRxiv preprint from the Zhou lab. It asks whether rare-variant associations with disease onset are the same ones that drive later progression. To test that, the authors built GATE-GENE, a gene-based time-to-event test meant to stay calibrated even with few carrier events and heavy censoring.

They applied it in UK Biobank and All of Us and found 107 exome-wide significant gene-disease associations across 300 onset phenotypes. The striking result is that onset signals and progression signals overlap very little.
Their simulations suggest that when sharing does show up, it comes mostly from overlapping downstream events, not true shared biology. A cross-biobank meta-analysis added 12 progression associations.

It's a preprint, and we only have a summary, so the details of calibration and ancestry makeup still need checking. But the warning holds: a gene that matters for getting a disease may not matter for how it unfolds.
The second paper, from the Vries lab in Genetic Epidemiology, asks whether rare and ultra-rare variants improve polygenic prediction of LDL cholesterol.

The authors built common- and rare-variant scores using TOPMed whole genomes and Global Lipids Genetics Consortium weights. They also built gene-based scores weighted by burden-test effects for loss-of-function, missense and regulatory masks, then tested everything in about 190,000 UK Biobank genomes.

The rare-variant score and the regulatory gene-burden score each added about half a percent of R squared beyond the common-variant score. The best combined model explained about nine point eight to ten percent of LDL variance.
So the gains are real but small, and it's a single, well-studied trait in one biobank. Both papers show that rare variants add information, just in narrower places than we might hope.
The takeaway: rare-variant effects depend on context, whether that's the stage of a disease or the gain on top of common variants, so measure them where they actually apply.

papers.title: Exome-wide rare-variant associations vary across disease trajectories
Exploring the Role of Low-Frequency and Rare Variants in the Genetic Risk Prediction of Low-Density Lipoprotein Cholesterol
